proof_used_steps.claim: Let $(f_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $(\mathcal B(S),d_\infty)$ and fix $s\in S$. For all $j,k$ one has $|f_j(s)-f_k(s)|\in\{|f_j(s')-f_k(s')|:s'\in S\}$ and therefore $|f_j(s)-f_k(s)|\le d_\infty(f_j,f_k)$ by [F1] and [F6]. Hence $(f_j(s))_j$ is a Cauchy sequence of reals, so it converges; define $f(s):=\lim_j f_j(s)\in\mathbb R$. This defines a function $f:S\to\mathbb R$.

Boundedness of $f$: since $(f_j)$ is Cauchy, there is $N$ with $d_\infty(f_j,f_N)\le1$ for all $j\ge N$; then $|f_j(s)|\le|f_N(s)|+1\le\sup_{s'}|f_N(s')|+1=:M$ for all $j\ge N$ and all $s$, where $M<\infty$ because $f_N$ is bounded ([F1], [F6]). For fixed $s$, the constant sequence $M$ has limit $M$ and $|f_j(s)|\le M$ for all $j\ge N$, so [F5] gives $|f(s)|\le M$. Thus $f\in\mathcal B(S)$.

Uniform error estimate: given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ with $d_\infty(f_j,f_k)\le\varepsilon$ for all $j,k\ge N$. Fix $j\ge N$ and $s\in S$; then $|f_k(s)-f_j(s)|\le d_\infty(f_k,f_j)\le\varepsilon$ for every $k\ge N$ ([F1], [F6]), and the sequence $k\mapsto|f_k(s)-f_j(s)|$ converges to $|f(s)-f_j(s)|$; [F5] gives $|f(s)-f_j(s)|\le\varepsilon$. Taking the supremum over $s$ in [F1] gives $d_\infty(f,f_j)\le\varepsilon$ for every $j\ge N$, so $f_j\to f$ in $(\mathcal B(S),d_\infty)$.

The space $(B_R(S),d_\infty)$ is complete: if $(f_j)$ is Cauchy in $(B_R(S),d_\infty)$, then by steps 2.1 and 3.1 its pointwise limit $f$ lies in $\mathcal B(S)$ and $f_j\to f$; for each $s$ one has $|f_j(s)|\le R$ for all $j$, so [F5] gives $|f(s)|\le R$; hence $f\in B_R(S)$ and the Cauchy sequence converges inside $B_R(S)$.

Conclusion. Clause 1 is proved by steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1: the pointwise limit of a Cauchy sequence of bounded functions is bounded (step 2.1) and is the uniform limit (step 3.1). Clause 2 is step 4.1, and clause 3 is step 1.2. For clause 4, take $S=\mathbb Z$: by the definitions of [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]] the space $\mathcal B(\mathbb Z)$ is exactly $\ell^\infty(\mathbb Z)$ and $d_\infty(f,g)=\sup_k|f_k-g_k|=\|f-g\|_\infty$, so clauses 1 and 2 give completeness of $\ell^\infty(\mathbb Z)$ and of each $B_R$, $R\ge0$; with $S=\mathbb N$ the same identifications give the one-sided statement, the argument being identical since it never uses any structure of the index set beyond its nonemptiness.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] Square roots ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]): every $u\ge0$ has a unique $u^{1/2}:=\sqrt u\ge0$ with $(\sqrt u)^2=u$; if $0\le u\le v$ then $\sqrt u\le\sqrt v$, since $\sqrt u,\sqrt v\ge0$ and $(\sqrt u)^2=u\le v=(\sqrt v)^2$; in particular $\sqrt{u^2}=u$ for $u\ge0$ and $\sqrt{x}>0$ for $x>0$. Also $\sqrt a\ge10$ because $a\ge100=10^2$ and $t\mapsto t^2$ is increasing on $[0,\infty)$.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] Order arithmetic on intervals ([[def-interval]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]): if $|x_j|\le R$ for $j\in\mathbb Z$ then $a-R-R\le a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}\le a+R+R$; and for reals $u\ge v>0$ one has $\sqrt{u}\ge\sqrt v>0$ by [F1].

proof_used_steps.claim: Constants: by [F1], $\sqrt a\ge10$, so $R=\sqrt a+3\ge13$ and $a-2R=a-2\sqrt a-6=(\sqrt a-1)^2-7\ge81-7=74$; hence $L=\sqrt{a-2R}\ge\sqrt{74}>1$ by [F1]. Further $R^2=a+6\sqrt a+9$ and $R^2-(a+2R)=a+6\sqrt a+9-a-2\sqrt a-6=4\sqrt a+3>0$, so $a+2R<R^2$ and [F1] gives $\sqrt{a+2R}<R$.

Well-definedness and self-mapping: let $s\in X_\pm$, $x\in B_R$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$. Since $|x_{n\pm1}|\le R$ by [F2], [F5] gives $a-2R\le a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}\le a+2R$; by step 1.1 this is a positive interval, so [F1] makes $\sqrt{a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}}$ a well-defined positive real, and $T_sx$ is a function $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$. Moreover $|(T_sx)_n|=|s_n|\sqrt{a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}}=\sqrt{a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}}\le\sqrt{a+2R}<R$ by [F4], [F1] and step 1.1. Taking the supremum over $n$ gives $\|T_sx\|_\infty\le\sqrt{a+2R}<R$, so $T_s(B_R)\subseteq B_R$.

Contraction: let $x,y\in B_R$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$, and put $u:=a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}$, $v:=a+y_{n-1}+y_{n+1}$; by step 1.1 both lie in $[a-2R,a+2R]\subseteq[L^2,\infty)$, so $\sqrt u,\sqrt v\ge L>0$ by [F1]. Then $$|\sqrt u-\sqrt v|=\frac{|u-v|}{\sqrt u+\sqrt v}\le\frac{|u-v|}{2L}\le\frac{|x_{n-1}-y_{n-1}|+|x_{n+1}-y_{n+1}|}{2L}\le\frac{\|x-y\|_\infty}{L},$$ where the first identity is the algebraic identity $u-v=(\sqrt u-\sqrt v)(\sqrt u+\sqrt v)$ ([F1], [F4]), the second inequality uses [F4] and [F5], and the last uses [F2]. Since $|(T_sx)_n-(T_sy)_n|=|\sqrt u-\sqrt v|$ by [F4], taking the supremum over $n$ gives $\|T_sx-T_sy\|_\infty\le\|x-y\|_\infty/L$, and $1/L<1$ by step 1.1.

Properties of the fixed point: fix $n$ and write $r:=\sqrt{a+x_{n-1}(s)+x_{n+1}(s)}>0$, so that $x_n(s)=s_nr$ by the fixed point equation. If $s_n=+1$ then $x_n(s)=r>0$, and if $s_n=-1$ then $x_n(s)=-r<0$; hence in both cases $\operatorname{sign}x_n(s)=s_n$ and $|x_n(s)|=r$. Squaring the fixed point equation gives $x_n(s)^2=r^2=a+x_{n-1}(s)+x_{n+1}(s)$, which is the recurrence, and $|x_n(s)|=r\ge L$ by step 1.1, [F1] and [F5].

facts.text: [F2] Absolute value and order ([[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]): $|uv|=|u||v|$; $|u-w|\ge|u|-|w|$; if $|u|\le k|v|$ and $0<k<1$ then $\max(|u|,|v|)=|v|$; if $|v|\le k|u|$ then $\max(|u|,|v|)=|u|$; and $k(4-k)>1$ for $0<k<1$.

proof_used_steps.claim: Constants: since $L\ge2$ and $0<k<1$, we have $2L-k\ge4-k>3$, so $\lambda=2L-k>1$ and $0<\rho=\lambda^{-2}<1$; moreover $k(2L-k)\ge k(4-k)>1$ by [F2], hence $1/\lambda<k$.

Unstable cone: let $(u,v)\in C^u_k$, so $|u|\le k|v|$ and $\max(|u|,|v|)=|v|$ by [F2]. Then $DF_a(z_n)(u,v)=(v,-u+2s_nv)$ and $|{-u}+2s_nv|\ge2|s_n||v|-|u|\ge(2L-k)|v|=\lambda|v|$ by [F2]. Also $|{-u}+2s_nv|\ge\lambda|v|\ge|v|$ since $\lambda>1$, so $\max(|v|,|{-u}+2s_nv|)\ge\lambda\max(|u|,|v|)$. Finally $|v|/|{-u}+2s_nv|\le1/\lambda<k$ whenever $v\ne0$, so the image is in $C^u_k$ (the case $v=0$ gives $u=0$ and image $0$).

Stable cone: let $(u,v)\in C^s_k$, so $|v|\le k|u|$ and $\max(|u|,|v|)=|u|$ by [F2]. Then $DF_a(z_n)^{-1}(u,v)=(2s_{n-1}u-v,u)$ and $|2s_{n-1}u-v|\ge2L|u|-|v|\ge(2L-k)|u|=\lambda|u|$; hence $\max(|2s_{n-1}u-v|,|u|)\ge\lambda\max(|u|,|v|)$ and $|u|/|2s_{n-1}u-v|\le1/\lambda<k$ whenever $u\ne0$, with the zero case trivial.

Slope contractions: let $|y|\ge L$ and $h,h'\in[-k,k]$; by step 1.1, $|2y-h|\ge2L-k=\lambda>0$ and $|2y-h'|\ge\lambda$, so $\Phi_y$ is defined on $[-k,k]$, $|\Phi_y(h)|\le1/\lambda\le k$, and $$|\Phi_y(h)-\Phi_y(h')|=\frac{|h-h'|}{|2y-h||2y-h'|}\le\lambda^{-2}|h-h'|=\rho|h-h'| .$$ The same computation with $\Psi_x$ proves the second assertion.

Unstable slopes, uniform bounds and contraction: define $h^{(0)}_n:=0$, $h^{(m+1)}_n:=\Phi_{s_{n-1}}(h^{(m)}_{n-1})$. By induction, step 2.3 gives $|h^{(m)}_n|\le1/\lambda$ for all $m\ge1$ and $n$, and $|h^{(m+1)}_n-h^{(m)}_n|\le\rho^m/\lambda$ for all $m\ge0$. Hence for $m'\ge m$, $$|h^{(m')}_n-h^{(m)}_n|\le\sum_{j=m}^{m'-1}\rho^j/\lambda\le\frac{\rho^m}{\lambda(1-\rho)},$$ uniformly in $n$. Thus $(h^{(m)}_n)_m$ is Cauchy with a bound independent of $n$; by [F3] and [F4] it converges to some $h_n$, and $|h_n|\le1/\lambda\le k$.

Stable slopes: the same argument with $r^{(0)}_n:=0$, $r^{(m+1)}_n:=\Psi_{s_n}(r^{(m)}_{n+1})$ gives $|r^{(m+1)}_n-r^{(m)}_n|\le\rho^m/\lambda$, limits $r_n\in[-k,k]$ satisfying $r_n=\Psi_{s_n}(r_{n+1})=1/(2s_n-r_{n+1})$.

Uniqueness: let $(\tilde h_n)$ be another family with $|\tilde h_n|\le k$ and $\tilde h_n=\Phi_{s_{n-1}}(\tilde h_{n-1})$ for all $n$. Comparing with the construction gives, by induction on $m$, $|\tilde h_n-h^{(m)}_n|\le\rho^m|\tilde h_{n-m}-h^{(0)}_{n-m}|\le\rho^m\cdot2k$ (step 2.3, [F2]); letting $m\to\infty$ and using [F3] gives $\tilde h_n=h_n$. The stable case is identical with the future-pointing iteration.

facts.text: [F4] Absolute value and order arithmetic ([[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]): $|uv|=|u||v|$, $|u+w|\le|u|+|w|$, and $\theta^{-n}>0$ for all $n$.

proof_used_steps.claim: Contraction: let $u,v\in\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$ and $b\in J$. For $n\ge1$ the arguments $z_{n-1},z_{n+1}$ of $M_{s_n}$ contain the errors $u_{n\pm1}$, and [F1] gives $$\bigl|(T_bu)_n-(T_bv)_n\bigr|\le c\bigl(|u_{n-1}-v_{n-1}|+|u_{n+1}-v_{n+1}|\bigr)\le\theta^n\,c(\theta^{-1}+\theta)\,\|u-v\|_\theta=\theta^n\,q\,\|u-v\|_\theta .$$ For $n=0$ only the argument $z_1$ varies, so $\bigl|(T_bu)_0-(T_bv)_0\bigr|\le c|u_1-v_1|\le q\|u-v\|_\theta$ because $c\theta\le q$. Multiplying by $\theta^{-n}$ and taking the supremum gives $\|T_bu-T_bv\|_\theta\le q\|u-v\|_\theta$.

Ball invariance: suppose $|b-b_*|\le(1-q)\bar\rho/c$ and $\|u\|_\theta\le\bar\rho$. Then for every $n$ the points $z_{n\pm1}=y_{n\pm1}+u_{n\pm1}$ lie in $J$ by the hypothesis $[y_n-\bar\rho,y_n+\bar\rho]\subseteq J$ (with $n\pm1$ in place of $n$) and [F4]. For $n\ge1$, using the reference recurrence of the statement, $$\bigl|(T_bu)_n\bigr|=\bigl|M_{s_n}(z_{n-1},z_{n+1})-M_{s_n}(y_{n-1},y_{n+1})\bigr|\le c\bigl(|u_{n-1}|+|u_{n+1}|\bigr)\le\theta^nq\,\|u\|_\theta\le\theta^nq\bar\rho .$$ For $n=0$, $(T_bu)_0=M_{s_0}(b,z_1)-M_{s_0}(b_*,y_1)$, so $|(T_bu)_0|\le c|b-b_*|+c|u_1|\le(1-q)\bar\rho+q\bar\rho=\bar\rho$. Hence $\|T_bu\|_\theta\le\bar\rho$.

Linearised equation: fix $b$ and put $z^*_k:=y_k+u_k(b)$ for $k\ge0$ and $z^*_{-1}:=b$. Define the affine map $L$ on $\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$ by $$(Ld)_n:=\partial_1M_{s_n}(z^*_{n-1},z^*_{n+1})\,d_{n-1}+\partial_2M_{s_n}(z^*_{n-1},z^*_{n+1})\,d_{n+1}\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (Ld)_0:=\partial_2M_{s_0}(b,z^*_1)\,d_1+\partial_1M_{s_0}(b,z^*_1),$$ where $d_{-1}:=1$ is held fixed. The homogeneous part $d\mapsto Ld-d_{-1}\text{-part}$ is a contraction of constant $q$ by the computation of step 1.1, so [F3] gives a unique $d(b)\in\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$ with $Ld(b)=d(b)$, i.e. the displayed system; taking the fixed point of the homogeneous contraction started at $0$ gives $\|d(b)\|_\theta\le c/(1-q)$ because the forcing $\partial_1M_{s_0}(b,z^*_1)e_0$ has norm at most $c$.

Taylor remainder: put $u':=u(b+h)$ and $\Delta:=u'-u(b)$. For $n\ge1$, [F1] applied at $z=(z^*_{n-1},z^*_{n+1})$ and $z'=(z'_{n-1},z'_{n+1})$ gives $$\bigl|(T_{b+h}u')_n-(T_bu)_n-\partial_1M_{s_n}\Delta_{n-1}-\partial_2M_{s_n}\Delta_{n+1}\bigr|\le K\bigl(|\Delta_{n-1}|+|\Delta_{n+1}|\bigr)^2\le 2K\bigl(|\Delta_{n-1}|^2+|\Delta_{n+1}|^2\bigr),$$ and multiplying by $\theta^{-n}$ bounds this by $2K\theta^{n}(\theta^{-2}+\theta^{2})\|\Delta\|^2_\theta$. For $n=0$ one has the analogous bound $K|\Delta_1|^2+K'h^2$ with $K'$ a bound for the second derivative of $b\mapsto M_{s_0}(b,z^*_1)$, obtained from [F1] applied in the first variable, so altogether $$\bigl\|u'-(T_bu)-\bigl[D_uT_b(u)\bigr]\Delta-D_bT_b(u)h\bigr\|_\theta\le C_0\bigl(\|\Delta\|_\theta^2+h^2\bigr)$$ with the constants absorbed into $C_0<\infty$.

Lipschitz dependence and a priori bound: for $u\in\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$ and $b,b'\in J$, $(T_{b'}u)_n=(T_bu)_n$ for $n\ge1$, while $\bigl|(T_{b'}u)_0-(T_bu)_0\bigr|\le c|b'-b|$; hence $\|T_{b'}u-T_bu\|_\theta\le c|b'-b|$ by [F1] and [F4]. Applying this with $u=u(b')$ and using [F3] gives $\|u(b')-u(b)\|_\theta\le q\|u(b')-u(b)\|_\theta+c|b'-b|$, hence $\|u(b')-u(b)\|_\theta\le c|b'-b|/(1-q)$. Taking $b'=b_*$ and using $u(b_*)=0$ (the zero sequence is the fixed point because $y$ itself solves the recurrence and $b=b_*$ produces the zero error) gives $\|u(b)\|_\theta\le c|b-b_*|/(1-q)$.

Differentiability: write $D_uT:=D_uT_b(u(b))$ and $D_bT:=D_bT_b(u(b))$ for the two partial derivatives of the map $(b,u)\mapsto T_bu$ at $(b,u(b))$. By step 3.2 applied to the fixed point equations $u(b+h)=T_{b+h}u(b+h)$ and $u(b)=T_bu(b)$, $$u(b+h)=u(b)+D_uT\,\Delta+D_bT\,h+R_1,\qquad \|R_1\|_\theta\le C_0\bigl(\|\Delta\|_\theta^2+h^2\bigr),$$ with $\Delta=u(b+h)-u(b)$. By step 2.2, $h\,d(b)=D_uT\,(h\,d(b))+D_bT\,h$; subtracting $h\,d(b)$ from the displayed equation and putting $R:=\Delta-h\,d(b)$ therefore yields $R=D_uT\,R+R_1$, whence $\|R\|_\theta\le q\|R\|_\theta+\|R_1\|_\theta$. By step 4.1, $\|\Delta\|_\theta\le c|h|/(1-q)$, so $\|R_1\|_\theta\le C_1h^2$ for $|h|$ small and hence $\|R\|_\theta\le C_1h^2/(1-q)$: that is, $u(b+h)=u(b)+h\,d(b)+O(h^2)$ in $\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$. This proves differentiability with derivative $d(b)$ and identifies it with the solution of clause 3.

Continuity of the derivative: by step 2.2 the difference of the linear operators at $b'$ and $b$ has coefficients $\partial_iM_{s_n}(z'_{n\pm1})-\partial_iM_{s_n}(z_{n\pm1})$, which tend to zero uniformly in $n$ as $b'\to b$ by uniform continuity of the $\partial_iM_u$ on the compact $J\times J$ and by the uniform estimate $|z'_k-z_k|\le c|b'-b|/(1-q)$ of step 4.1; the same holds for the forcing. Applying the difference estimate of step 4.1 to the fixed points $d(b'),d(b)$ of the affine maps gives $\|d(b')-d(b)\|_\theta\to0$.

The curve: the map $b\mapsto\gamma(b)=(b,y_0+u_0(b))$ has components the identity and the affine function of $u_0$, and $b\mapsto u_0(b)$ is continuously differentiable by steps 5.1 and 5.2 with derivative $d_0(b)$; hence $\gamma$ is $C^1$ with the displayed derivative ([F5]). The bound $|d_0(b)|\le\|d(b)\|_\theta\le c/(1-q)$ is step 2.2.
